question: Can language models be fine-tuned, without human labels, to produce fewer factual errors in long-form generation?
hypothesis: Preference pairs ranked by automatic truthfulness scores (reference-based or model-confidence-based) and optimised with DPO will reduce factual errors more than RLHF or factuality decoding.
contributions: A straightforward approach to optimizing language models for factuality in long-form generation without human annotation
A reference-free truthfulness estimator based on the model's own confidence over extracted atomic claims
Evidence that factuality tuning beats RLHF and composes with decoding methods such as DOLA

method.summary: Sample n responses per prompt at temperature 1.0 from an SFT/base model, score each by FactScore (Wikipedia-supported fraction of atomic claims) or by model confidence (largest-bin fraction of 20 resampled answers to GPT-3.5-generated questions), label the higher-scoring response of each pair as preferred, then run DPO. Evaluated on generated biographies and medical QA with FactScore counts, human and GPT-4 checks.
method.task: preference optimisation for factuality of long-form generation

datasets.name: Biographies
datasets.size: 355 entities (296 train, 59 test), 10 responses per entity, 1 prompt per entity
datasets.source: prompts generated with GPT-3.5; answers sampled from Llama-1-7B with a few-shot prompt; entities have Wikipedia pages

datasets.name: MedicalQA
datasets.size: 200 medical conditions (150 train, 50 test), 6 questions per condition, 6 responses per question
datasets.source: prompts generated with GPT-3.5; answers sampled from Llama-1-7B with a few-shot prompt; conditions have Wikipedia pages

other.note: also samples the confidence answers for all experiments

other.use: also baseline RLHF model with human labels
claim extraction, claim-to-question rewrite, relevance check, optional equivalence check

training.objective: DPO loss (Eq. 3) on automatically ranked pairs; SFT stage uses all model responses as targets

other.pairs: m*C(n,2)-k pairs, k = pairs with equal scores

inference.decoding: temperature sampling to build preference data; test-time sampling 'in the normal manner' (not specified)
inference.samples: 20 resampled answers per claim for confidence (12 in Table 5 ablation); 10 (bios) / 6 (MedQA) responses per prompt
inference.prompting: few-shot prompting for models not fine-tuned
inference.retrieval: FactScore retrieves from Wikipedia at training and eval time only; none at inference

parameters.confidence_metric: fraction of samples in the largest semantic bin (max conf) or entropy over bins
parameters.equivalence: heuristic string match (non-stop-word overlap) or GPT-3.5
parameters.fact_extraction: atomic claims by GPT-3.5, or named entities (spaCy/nltk noun chunks)

metrics.name: # Correct
metrics.definition: number of correct (and relevant for MedQA) facts per response per FactScore

metrics.name: # Incorrect
metrics.definition: number of inaccurate facts per response per FactScore

metrics.name: % Correct
metrics.definition: proportion of correct relevant facts out of total extracted facts

eval.protocol: FactScore automated counts on test entities; human check via Prolific; GPT-4 error counts. Number of seeds or runs not stated; no significance tests.

prompts.purpose: GPT-3.5 atomic fact to question (biography template)
prompts.text: I will provide a statement containing one atomic fact related to [NAME] or people around [HIM/HER]. Please rephrase the following statement into a specific question testing knowledge of the key fact in the statement. For example: ... Statement: [STATEMENT] Question:

prompts.purpose: GPT-3.5 atomic fact to question (MedicalQA template)
prompts.text: I will provide a statement containing one atomic fact about the medical condition [CONDITION]. Please rephrase the following statement into a specific question testing knowledge of the key fact in the statement. For example: ... Statement: [STATEMENT] Question:

evidence.where: no optimizer, learning rate, batch size, beta or epochs are printed anywhere in the text

results.setup: Llama-2-7B, FactTune vs Llama-2-Chat, biographies; 40% for MedQA
results.quote: At 7B scale, compared to Llama-2-chat, we observe 58% and 40% reduction

results.claim: Professional fact-checkers needed about 9 minutes per biography and $2,000 for 505 biographies.

limits: Only 7B models tested; scaling to larger models left open (Conclusion).
Two new tasks (biographies, medical QA) that the authors say do not fully cover factuality scenarios.
How to combine factuality rankings with typical RLHF rewards is left open.
Training hyperparameters (optimizer, lr, beta, batch size, epochs, hardware) are not reported, nor seeds or significance tests.
Outputs become terser, less conversational and not chronological after tuning (Sec 4.1, App A.2).
FactScore is both preference signal and main metric; mitigated by human and GPT-4 checks.
GPT-4 equivalence checking was not run for cost reasons.
DOLA stacking hurt Llama-2 on biographies.
